Getting started with GateLabR

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

GateLabR is a desktop-style Shiny app for hand-gating flow and mass cytometry (CyTOF) data directly on SingleCellExperiment objects — a free, MIT-licensed alternative to round-tripping through Cytobank or FlowJo. Gates, populations, scales and figure settings live inside the object’s metadata(), so your gated data is the record.

📸 Screenshot: the full app with the gating biplot in the centre, gate/population lists on the right. — add man/figures/overview.png

1. Install and launch

Install once as a package (Bioconductor dependencies are resolved automatically; install BiocManager first if you don’t have it):

# install.packages(c("remotes", "BiocManager"))
remotes::install_github("david-priest/GateLabR")
library(GateLabR)
launchGatingApp()

Or run from a clone:

source("path/to/GateLabR/launch.R")
launchGatingApp()

launchGatingApp() prints which copy it’s launching (installed package vs source clone). It opens in your browser.

2. Get your data in

GateLabR opens on an R object, not on FCS files: a SingleCellExperiment or a flowWorkspace GatingSet. Pass the object, or call launchGatingApp() with no argument to pick from the SCEs in your session.

launchGatingApp(my_sce)          # a SingleCellExperiment
launchGatingApp(my_gs)           # a flowWorkspace GatingSet
launchGatingApp()                # pick from the SCEs in your session

A CyTOF SingleCellExperiment comes from CATALYST’s prepData(). FCS files from a flow cytometer are assembled into either object with flowCore and flowWorkspace:

library(flowCore)
library(flowWorkspace)
fs <- read.flowSet(path = "fcs/", pattern = "\\.fcs$", truncate_max_range = FALSE)

# A GatingSet keeps the files' events on disk, compensated and transformed in place.
# Compensate before transforming: a GatingSet cannot be uncompensated.
gs <- GatingSet(fs)
compensate(gs, spillover(fs[[1]])$SPILL)                # the matrix the files record
fluor <- grep("-A$", colnames(gs), value = TRUE)
fluor <- setdiff(fluor, grep("^(FSC|SSC)", fluor, value = TRUE))
transform(gs, estimateLogicle(gs[[1]], fluor))          # logicle per channel, W from the data
launchGatingApp(gs)

# A SingleCellExperiment holds the events as columns and the channels as rows. Keep the
# uncompensated values as `counts`; GateLabR compensates in the app and stores the result as
# a second assay.
library(SingleCellExperiment)
events <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(fs), function(i) exprs(fs[[i]])))
sample_id <- rep(sampleNames(fs), fsApply(fs, nrow))
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(
  assays = list(counts = t(events)),
  colData = DataFrame(sample_id = sample_id),
  rowData = DataFrame(channel_name = colnames(events),
                      marker_name = unname(markernames(fs[[1]])[colnames(events)]))
)
metadata(sce)$spillover <- spillover(fs[[1]])$SPILL     # offered in the Compensation tab
launchGatingApp(sce)

On a GatingSet, the hierarchy it holds opens as the app’s gates, drawn in the transformed space the object evaluates them in, and “Save to GatingSet” writes the populations back to the hierarchy in place (see ?launchReactGateLab). On an SCE, flow data is drawn on a per-channel logicle for fluorescence and linear scatter (editable W and cofactor); CyTOF uses arcsinh (cofactor 5).

3. The layout

Panel Contents
Left Sample filter, scale controls, FCS / GatingML / workspace import-export, UMAP
Centre Interactive plot — tabs: Gating · Strategy · Illustration · Statistics · Panel
Right Gates list, population tree, bulk-rename

4. Draw gates

On the Gating tab, pick the X/Y channels (click the axis labels) and choose a tool from the toolbar:

  • Rect — drag a rectangle.
  • Poly — click vertices; click the first point (or near it) to close.
  • Quad — click once to drop a quadrant crosshair (see below).

Drag a vertex to adjust it; a live x, y readout follows the cursor. Gates get a name and an optional population on creation.

📸 Screenshot: a polygon gate being drawn, with the live vertex readout. — add man/figures/draw-gate.png

5. Build populations

Populations are boolean combinations of gates (AND / OR, include / exclude), shown as a tree on the right with live counts and percentages. Click a population to make it active (blue) and gate within it; the biplot and counts follow.

Tips:

  • Arrow keys move the active population up/down the list.
  • The left-column checkboxes let you display several populations’ events at once (a banner tells you which are shown); clicking a gate badge outlines that gate in every population it appears in.

📸 Screenshot: the population tree with a small hierarchy and live counts. — add man/figures/population-tree.png

6. Quadrant gates

The Quad tool drops a crosshair that splits the X/Y plane into four populations at once (e.g. CD4- CD8+, CD4+ CD8+, CD4+ CD8-, CD4- CD8-), each labelled with its count and %. Drag the centre to move all four together; deleting the quadrant gate removes its four populations (and vice-versa).

📸 Screenshot: a quadrant gate with the four corner counts. — add man/figures/quadrant.png

7. Compensation (flow)

For conventional flow data carrying a spillover matrix, toggle Apply compensation to linearly compensate fluorescence channels from the embedded $SPILLOVER. (CyTOF and pre-compensated/spectral data don’t need it.)

On a SingleCellExperiment the matrix lives in metadata(sce)$spillover, a numeric matrix with the source channels as row names and the receiver channels as column names, as flowCore::spillover() returns it; that is the one documented name, read first (the older spillover_matrix, spilloverMatrix and sm are still read after it); a matrix applied in the app is kept with the workspace record, not written back to this slot. A GatingSet carries its applied matrix itself (gh_get_compensations()).

📸 Screenshot: the compensation toggle + matrix viewer. — add man/figures/compensation.png

8. Figures: Strategy & Illustration

  • Strategy lays out your gating hierarchy as a multi-panel figure.
  • Illustration renders a grid of biplots/histograms across populations and channels — including a stacked ridgeline mode with a black→yellow heat-gradient fill, adjustable overlap and column spacing. The Heatmap option summarizes median or mean transformed expression for each selected population (rows) and channel (columns), with no scaling, per-channel or per-population 0–1 scaling, or per-channel z-scores; black→yellow, viridis and blue→white→yellow→red palettes are available.

Both export to SVG (vector, Illustrator-friendly) and PNG.

📸 Screenshot: a ridgeline illustration across markers. — add man/figures/ridgeline.png

9. Export & persistence

  • Populations → colData (Export Population) for downstream diffcyt, CATALYST, or any SCE-aware analysis.
  • FCS export of gated events (defaults to the raw counts assay).
  • Gating-ML 2.0 import/export to exchange gates with Cytobank. FlowJo does not read Gating-ML; it uses its own .wsp format.
  • Workspace is embedded in metadata(sce)$gatelab_workspace, with a metadata(sce)$gating_workspace mirror kept for the previous interface; saveRDS() the object (or export a portable .rds) and re-loading restores everything.
  • Axes are kept on the rows: rowData(sce)$gatelab_transform holds the transform each channel was drawn on at the last save (gatelabTransforms(sce) reads it), as a GatingSet keeps its transforms with its data.
saveRDS(sce, "gated.rds")   # gates, populations, scales — all preserved

10. For flowWorkspace and openCyto users

A GatingSet is gated in the same app, and everything stays in flowWorkspace’s terms. The hierarchy the object holds opens as the app’s gates, each evaluated in the transformed space the object evaluates it in (logicle, FlowJo’s biexponential and log, arcsinh), with the same counts; the matrix the object carries is shown; pData() columns are the sample metadata and colour the plots. “Save to GatingSet” writes the populations back to the hierarchy, in place, and save_gs() keeps them.

library(flowWorkspace)
gs <- load_gs("gated/")                        # or CytoML::flowjo_to_gatingset(ws, name = 1),
                                               # cytobank_to_gatingset(...), or a GatingSet(fs)
                                               # you compensated and transformed yourself
launchGatingApp(gs)                            # draw, then "R host ▸ Save to GatingSet"

gs_get_pop_paths(gs)                           # the tree, the app's populations included
gh_pop_get_count(gs[[1]], "/Lymphocytes/CD4")  # counts as flowWorkspace computes them
gh_pop_get_gate(gs[[1]], "/Lymphocytes/CD4")   # a rectangleGate, polygonGate or ellipsoidGate
ggcyto::autoplot(gs[[1]], "/Lymphocytes/CD4")  # drawn by ggcyto as any other node
gatelabPopulations(gs)                         # or the GateLabR readers, as for an SCE
save_gs(gs, "gated/")                          # the hierarchy and the GateLab record together

What to expect:

  • A rectangle drawn in the app returns as a rectangleGate whatever the axes’ transforms; a polygon or ellipse returns as its gate when it was drawn in the object’s own transform space (the app’s axes take the object’s transforms at the first open, so this is the usual case on a logicle or arcsinh object). A quadrant, a population excluding a gate, or a polygon drawn in another space returns as its exact per-sample membership: a booleanFilter-class node that gh_pop_get_indices() reads like any other, with GateLab’s count. The console says which populations went which way.
  • Every gate written is recomputed by flowWorkspace and compared with the app’s membership; one that selects other events is replaced by the membership, so a node never holds different events in R than it showed in the app.
  • The object is modified in place, as gs_pop_add() modifies it. A matrix applied in the app’s Compensation tab is applied with flowWorkspace::compensate(), in place and to the whole object, when the object is writable, uncompensated and untransformed — the uncompensated values are then gone from it, as after compensate() at the prompt. A GatingSet from load_gs() is read-only on its data, and compensation precedes transformation, so for those compensate in R before launching; the app says which applies.
  • A FlowJo-derived object’s biexponential channels open on FlowJo’s biexponential at the object’s parameters (the Scales tab offers it beside logicle and arcsinh), built from cytolib’s own table, so the axis and the gates are flowWorkspace’s to five thousandths of a channel.
  • Only the active tree is written to the hierarchy; parked hierarchies stay in the GateLab record (the GATELAB_WORKSPACE keyword on every sample).

The other direction is gatelabGatingSet(): an SCE gated in the app becomes a GatingSet, its samples as cytoframes from the assay the workspace was drawn on, its channels on the transforms the object states, and every population of the active hierarchy written as “Save to GatingSet” writes them, so flowWorkspace recomputes the gates, ggcyto draws them and CytoML exports them. The GateLab record goes along as the keyword, so launchGatingApp() on the result opens the same workspace.

gs <- gatelabGatingSet(sce)                    # after "Save to SCE"
gs_get_pop_paths(gs)                           # the SCE's populations as nodes
gatelabPopulations(gs)                         # the same memberships as gatelabPopulations(sce)
save_gs(gs, "from-sce/")
